On the Concordance of the Evangelists, one book. A Correctory of the Decree, three books. On Heresies, to the cardinal of Albano, one book. On the books of the Physics, eight books. Questions on the Soul, one book. He also composed many other things which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1320, and died on 21 August, buried at Avignon.

John of Alier, of Toulouse, thirteenth prior general of the whole order, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in talent, knowledge, and eloquence, also outstanding in life and conduct, and a notable preserver of regular discipline, wrote a distinguished volume on the Sentences, four books; a notable Ecclesiastical Reading, one book; and certain other things which I have not yet found. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1330, and lies buried in his own convent at Toulouse.

[Petrus?] de Casa, of the province of Aquitaine, after the resignation of John of Alier the fourteenth prior general of the whole order; then bishop of Vaison, and finally patriarch of Jerusalem; a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, left certain splendid volumes of his talent, among which these are reported: On the Sentences, seven books; Sermons for the season and on the saints, two books; also a notable Reading on the book of the Politics; and certain other things which are hidden from us. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1330. He died on the day before the Nones of August, radiant with miracles.

John Walsigram, prior provincial of England, a very learned man in the divine Scriptures, an acute philosopher, and doctor of sacred theology of Paris, wrote notably on the Sentences, seven books; Various Questions and quodlibets. He also composed some other things which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Simon of Speyer, a Teuton by nation, prior provincial of all Germany, doctor of Paris, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote on the Sentences, seven books; also various Sermons; and certain lectures on the divine volumes. In addition he is said to have written some other things, but they have not come into our hands. He died under Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340, in the eighth indiction, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, buried at Cologne in his own convent.

Peter Raymond de Graffa, a Gaul by nation, of the convent of Tarsac in the province of Narbonne, fifteenth prior general, a learned and devout man, wrote many splendid volumes, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these the following are extant: On the Sentences, eight books. He also gathered the various statutes of his order into one volume, and divided the same collections into sixty rubrics. But he also composed certain other things which have not come to our knowledge. He died in the year of the Lord 1357, in the tenth indiction, under Pope Innocent VI, buried at Montpellier, in the sixteenth year of his office as general.

John Baconthorpe, an Englishman by nation, prior provincial of England, doctor of Paris, a man most learned in every respect, a very celebrated philosopher, jurist, and theologian, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote many splendid little works, among which the following are reported: On the Sentences, seven books; On the Gospel of Matthew, one book; On the Gospel of Mark, one book; On the Gospel of Luke, one book; On the Gospel of John, one book; On the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books; On the Acts of the Apostles, one book; Various Disputed Questions, one book; Mirror of His Order, one book; Defense of His Order, one book; On Aristotle’s Metaphysics, in two volumes, twelve books; On the Soul, seven books; also On the books of the Ethics, one book. In addition he composed many other things which have not come to my knowledge. He also produced various explanations on the books of blessed Augustine On the Trinity and The City of God, and on Anselm’s Why God Became Man and On the Incarnation of the Word; in all of these he magnificently exercised his talent. He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1345.

Aulus of Perugia, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and also excellently trained in secular letters, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, published certain little works of great authority, by which he commended his name to posterity. Of these there is extant an outstanding volume on the Sentences, eight books; also Various Questions, one book; and certain other things. He flourished at Paris under Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1343.

John Balistarii, a Catalan, the sixteenth prior general of the whole order, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and an acute investigator of secular philosophy, excellent in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain very notable volumes, by which he destined his name for posterity. Of these the following are extant: On the Sentences, seven books; Constitutions of His Order, one book; On the Last Times, to the pope, one book; and certain other things. He died in the year of the Lord 1377, in the twelfth indiction, on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, and was buried in the convent of Majorca.

Peter Rimi of Perpignan, a Catalan by homeland, a very learned man, doctor of sacred Scripture, profound in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote an outstanding volume on the Sentences, eight books; also On the Whole Psalter, one book. In addition he composed various and elegant sermons, which have not come into our hands.

Berenus of Boyo, a Breton by nation, a man most skilled in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, an interpreter of the sacred letters and a profound Parisian doctor, is said to have fashioned several very notable volumes, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these there is extant an outstanding work on the Sentences, seven books; Various Questions; and other things which are hidden from us.

John de Regno, a Gaul by nation, of the convent of Toulouse, a learned doctor in the holy Scriptures, subtle in intellect and ready in eloquence, wrote on the Sentences, eight books; On the Gospel of Matthew, one book; Sermons on the Season and on the Saints, two books; also a Lenten Book, one book; and certain other things.

Peter Thomas, bishop of Pax and afterward patriarch of Constantinople, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, most holy in life and conduct, since indeed he shone with many miracles both while alive and after death. He is said to have written several very notable little works, by which he usefully exercised his intellect. Of these the following are reported: On the Sentences, seven books; On the Most Pure Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, one book; also Various Sermons, one book; and certain letters to various persons. In 1366, in the third indiction, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, distinguished by miracles.

Osbert, an Englishman by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently trained in secular philosophy, of acute and forceful intellect, of scholastic eloquence, ready and subtle in debating and resolving questions of the Scriptures, wrote a most elegant volume on the Sentences, four books; Various Disputed Questions, one book; also diverse Sermons, one book. In addition he is said to have written several other things, which we do not know.

Thilmannus, of the convent of Aachen, a German by nation, prior provincial of Lower Germany, an outstanding professor of sacred letters, excellent in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, an excellent declaimer of sermons, wrote on the Sentences, four books; On the Gospel of Matthew, a notable lecture, which he read publicly at Cologne in the convent, one book; also various sermons; and certain other things. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1370.

Heinrich Dolendorp, a German by nation, before Thilmannus prior provincial of Lower Germany, a learned and erudite man and a very celebrated declaimer, excellent in intellect and scholastic in eloquence, a most keen debater of questions, wrote a notable work on the Sentences, seven books; also various and useful sermons; and certain other things. He died and was buried in the convent of Cologne, in the year of the Lord 1356.

In the third indiction, on the fourth day before the Ides of February.

Philip Riboti, provincial prior of Catalonia, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in intellect, clear in speech, and a careful moderator of regular discipline. Among other monuments of his talent he wrote a distinguished work on the origin and progress of his order, which he entitled On the Special Deeds of the Carmelite Brothers, in ten books. He is also said to have composed some other works, which have not come into our hands.

Robert of Monstrolo, a Gaul by nationality, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, once an ornament of the University of Paris. He wrote on the Sentences, in three books; a notable lecture on the epistles of Paul, in fourteen books; various questions, in one book; sermons also on the season and on the saints, in two books. He is also said to have written some other works, which I have not yet seen.

John Fust, lector of the convent of Kreuznach and afterward prior of Strasbourg, German by nationality, born from the county of Sponheim: a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, a very celebrated preacher of sermons. Among other things he wrote elegant sermons on the season, in two books; also on the saints, in two books; sermons for Lent, in two books; and other things which are hidden from us.

John of Hildesheim, born from the city of Saxony, lector of the convent there, devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters also; a distinguished philosopher and poet, practiced in verse and prose, a very famous preacher of sermons to the people. He wrote little works not to be despised in reading, of which the following are reported: to Florentius, bishop of Munster in Westphalia, on the translation of the Three Kings into the city of Cologne, in one book; also a pleasant and useful chronicle, in one book; a defense of his order, in one book; On the Fountain of Life, in one book; Against the One Painting Shameful Things, in one book; a metrical work on monsters in the church, in one book; letters to various persons, in one book; sermons on the season and on the saints, in two books. He also published some other works, which have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1370, and composed various epigrams in verse.

John Golein, a Norman by nationality, prior of Rouen: a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and sufficiently learned in secular letters; subtle in intellect and clear in speech. He wrote little works of authority not to be spurned, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there survive: on the Sentences, in four books; on the office of the Mass, in one book; also various questions; and, as is reported, certain other works.

John Taceffale, English by nationality, of the Norwich convent, a learned man and greatly erudite in the holy Scriptures as well as in law and philosophy, ready in intellect and fit for preaching sermons to the people. He wrote on the Sentences, in three books; a notable lecture on the Apocalypse, in one book; also various sermons to the people. He published some other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge. Finally sent to Rome, he died there.

Ronald of Bissalis, [galtetienẜ]: a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures and clear in speech, not ignorant of rhetoric; profound in intellect and [unclear] ... notable, in one book; also various sermons to the people. He published some other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge. Finally sent to Rome, he died there.

John Horuby, English by nationality, a copious and learned doctor in the holy Scriptures, subtle in intellect and a very acute disputant of questions. He is said to have composed some splendid little works, by which the vein of his abundant talent made him known also to posterity. Of these there survives a work defending the antiquity of his order, in one book; also various sermons; and certain other works. He flourished in the university of Cantha[unclear].

[unclear]brigen[sis]. In the year of the Lord 1373, where he composed various works.

Franciscus Martini, a Catalan by nation, of the convent of Barcelona, was a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures. In delivering sermons to the people he was of excellent talent. He is said to have written several little works, in which his profound knowledge is shown. Of these the following are extant: On the conception of blessed Mary, ever virgin, one book; A compendium in honor of his order, seven books; and certain other things. He died in the aforesaid convent in the year of the Lord 1380.

Franciscus de Bachone, of the convent of Gerona, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and an acute disputant, wrote a distinguished volume on the Sentences, three books; also a certain Summa for preachers, one book. He is also said to have composed many other things, which have not come into our hands.

Johannes Deciminetho, lector of the convent of Metz, a Frenchman by nation, a man zealous and very learned in the divine writings, outstanding in talent and clear in eloquence, an eminent declaimer of popular sermons, wrote The Mirror of the Institution of His Order, one book; Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, one book; also Sermons on the Saints, one book; Sermons through Lent, one book. He is also said to have composed several other things, but they have not yet come to my notice.

Johannes Nobleth, a Frenchman by nation, of the convent of Paris, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently trained in secular letters, a notable philosopher and physician, wrote certain very distinguished little works of his talent, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of their number the following are reported: a distinguished work which he entitled Centilogium, one book; On the Gospel of John, one book. He is also said to have compiled commentaries and lectures on many other books of the Bible, which have not come to my notice.

Nicolaus Dorhm, an Englishman by nation, a doctor of Oxford, learned in the holy writings and subtly trained in Aristotelian philosophy, acute in intellect and forceful, a notable disputant in scholastic questions, wrote On the Sentences, three books; also Determinations of Various Questions, one book; a Table of the Originals. Besides these, he is said to have written many things, which have not come to me.

Johannes Marre, an Englishman by nation, a doctor of Oxford, zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures, subtle and forceful in intellect, wrote, among other little works of his exercise, Determinations against the Wycliffite Heretics, one book. He is also said to have written many other things, but they have not yet come to my notice.

Johannes de Gluel, a German by nation, prior of the convent of Cologne, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, clear in intellect, devout in life and conduct, wrote Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, one book; also Sermons on the Saints, one book; Sermons through Lent, one book. He also published several other things, which have not come to my notice. He flourished in his convent of Cologne, where he was also buried.

Walterus Disse, an Englishman by nation, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and a most celebrated declaimer of popular sermons, subtle in intellect and practiced in eloquence, wrote little works of no contemptible reading, of which the following are reported: Against the Lollards, one book; On the Schism, one book; On Certain Psalms, one book; Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, one book; also Sermons on the Saints, one book; and certain other things which have not come to my notice. He was the nuncio and legate of Pope Boniface IX in the kingdoms of England, Spain, Portugal, Navarre, Aragon, and in the regions of Gascony, preaching the cross against heretics and schismatics. He flourished under the emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1390, and was buried in the convent of Norwich.

Philippus de Ferrarla, a Sicilian by nation, bishop, as some maintain, of Patti, a most celebrated doctor of sacred theology, clear in intellect and profound in knowledge, an eminent declaimer of sermons, wrote very

Icolaus ritzonis cōuentus cathanensis natione n siculus. et prior ꝓvincialis scilie. doctor theolo- gus gymnasij bononienẜ. in declamandis ad po pulū sermonibus excellentis ingenij. scripsit dum adhuc bononie lr̄is operā daret. sermones elegantes de tꝑe li.i. Sermones quoqꝫ de sanctis li.i. Duo insuꝑ quadragesi malia composuisse dicitur: quoꝝ lectio declamatoribus vtilis iudicatur. Alia quoqꝫ nōnulla edidit: que ad noti- ciam meā non venerūt. Ohannes campscon̄. natione anglicus. vir in di uinis scripturis studiosus et eruditus. et secularis ph̕ie non ignarus. ingenio prestans et clarus elo quio. declamator sermonū popularum excellentissimus. Scripsit ad vtilitatem legentiū sermone de tempore li.i. Sermones quoqꝫ de sanctis li.i. Cetera que composuit ad noticiā meā non venerūt. Ohānes schonhoven na cōne theutonicus. prior cōuentus mechilinienẜ. vir in diuinis scripruris studiosus et longa exercitatione doctus. ingenio subtilis et promptus eloquio. in declandis ad populū sermonibus excellentis ingenij . scripsit notable opus in duobus voluminibus secundū ordinē alphabeti qd̓ p̄no tauit polipodion. p̄dicatoribus verbi dei valde accōmo- dum li. ij. Einricus de andernacho natione theutonicus. coloniensis dioceẜ. vir tam in scripturis diuinis

notable sermons on the season, one book; likewise sermons on the saints, one book; and certain other things. He flourished in the kingdom of Sicily, preaching before the king and others, not without profit to all.

Richard Lavinham, English by nation, doctor of sacred letters at Oxford, a subtle man and of vigorous talent, an acute disputant of questions and an outstanding declaimer of sermons, wrote certain excellent little works by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these the following are extant: Determinations against the Lollards, one book; likewise notable determinations on behalf of the book of the Revelations of Saint Bridget, which he read publicly in the schools of Oxford and London, one book. He also began a distinguished work on the foundation of his order, which, prevented by death, he did not complete. He also composed some things in logic and physics, which have not come into our hands.

Richard Maidescon, English by nation, doctor of sacred Scripture of the Oxford school, excellent in talent and renowned for eloquence, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, is said to have forged certain excellent little works by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant: Against the Lollards, one book; sermons on the season, one book; likewise sermons on the saints, one book; and various questions. In addition he composed several other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

William Talisfordie, English by nation, doctor of holy Scriptures of the Cambridge school, an educated and studious man, subtle in talent, devout in life and conduct, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, wrote very notable sermons on the season, one book; likewise sermons on the saints, one book. He also composed various readings of the Scriptures, which he read in the aforesaid school.

Thomas Lombe, English by nation, a most celebrated doctor of sacred letters of the Oxford school, a man renowned for wisdom and learning, subtle in talent and an acute disputant of scholastic questions, wrote against the Lollards and Wycliffites, one book; On the Incarnation of the Word, one book. He is said also to have written other little works, which I have not yet seen.

Nicholas Ritzonis, of the convent of Catania, Sicilian by nation, and provincial prior of Sicily, doctor of theology of the Bologna school, of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people, wrote, while he was still devoting himself to letters at Bologna, elegant sermons on the season, one book; likewise sermons on the saints, one book. He is said in addition to have composed two Lenten works, the reading of which is judged useful for preachers. He also published several other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

John Campscon, English by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, excellent in talent and renowned for eloquence, a most excellent declaimer of popular sermons, wrote for the benefit of readers sermons on the season, one book; likewise sermons on the saints, one book. The rest that he composed have not come to my knowledge.

John Schonhoven, German by nation, prior of the convent of Mechelen, a man studious in the divine Scriptures and learned by long practice, subtle in talent and ready in eloquence, of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people, wrote a notable work in two volumes according to alphabetical order, which he entitled Polipodion, very suitable for preachers of the word of God, two books. He also published various sermons on the season and on the saints, and certain other things.

Blasius Andernarij, French by nation, a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of the secrets of letters, wrote several excellent volumes by which he made known to posterity also the sharpness of his talent. Of these there is extant a celebrated work on the Sentences, four books; likewise various questions disputed in the schools. But the rest that he composed have by no means come to our knowledge.

Henry of Andernach, German by nation, of the diocese of Cologne, a man both in the divine Scriptures

24
q̃ꝫ in secularibus scientijs studiosus et eruditus. ingenio promptus et disputator acutus: scripsit volumen insigne suꝑ sententias li.uiij.Sermones de tempore li.i.Sermo nes quoqꝫ de sanctis li.i.Questiones ph̄ie.Sed et alia quedā composuit: que ad me non venerūt. Tephanus anglicus doctor oxouiensis et prior ꝓuincialis anglē.vir in diuinis scripturis erudi tus et secularis ph̄ie non ignarus.ingenio p̄stās et clarus eloquio:non minus vita q̃ꝫ erudicōne decorus Scripsit contra lolhardos li.i.Sermones tam de tem pore q̃ꝫ de sanctī circulū anni notabiles li.ij.Quaestio nes quoqꝫ varias li.i.Repertoriū argumentoꝝ suoꝝ li.i.Lecturas etiā quasdam notabiles in biblie libros edidit cū alijs multis que me latent. Rnoldus de austtia natione theuconicus cōuen tus venenẜ.et gymnasij eiusdem vrbis doctor in diuinis scripturus valde eruditus.et in seculari ph̄ia notabiliter doctus: ingenio subtilis et disputator questionum scolasticaliū egregius.fertur nōnulla p̄clara scripsisse opuscula: quibus memoriā sui posteris cōmen dauit.Equibꝫ extat volumen insigne suꝑ sentētias li.iiij.Sermones quoqꝫ et varie questiones.Claruit in p̄fato gymnasio weneni:vbi et dictā lecturam suā libri senten tiarum publice legit. Ohannes brammart natione theutonicus.con uentus aquenẜ.prior prouincialis inferioris ale manie doctor parisienẜ.in scripturis diuinis stu diosus et eruditus.ingenio subtilis et cōpositus eloquio.vita et conuersatione deuotus.scripsit insigne opus super sententias quattuoꝛ libros continens.quod parisius cō pleuit Anno domini Millesimo.ccc.lxxx.Jndictioneter cia.Incipit autē sic.Uerbum domini super iohannem.Sermones quoqꝫet varias questiones.Moritur in cō uentu coloniensi sepultus.Anno domini.D.cccc.vij.Jndictione.xv. m Ichael de bononia.natione ītalus prior genera lis.vir in diuinis scripturis studiosus et eruditus et seculariū lr̄aꝝ non ignarus.ingenio clarus et disertus eloquio.scripsit multa p̄clara opuscula: quibus memoriā sui posteris cōmendauit.Equibꝫ subiecta ferū tur.Sup̄ sentētias li.iij.Sed et questiones sentētiay li.i.Tabula sententiarū li.i.In totū psalterium opus grande li.i.Jn euangeliu mathei li.i.Jn euangelium luce.li.i.Tabula moraliū gregorij pape in iob li.i.Tabula super decreto li.i.De purissima conceptione beate marie semp virginis.li.i.Sermones varij li.i.Quadragesimale notabile li.i.Jn multos etiā libros aristotelis cōmentatus est Jn valeriū quoqꝫ maximū.Jn ph̓ia.in iure canonico.et in oratoria similiter varia scripsit.Et ml̓ta alia que ad me non venerūt.Moritur bononie ante summū altare sui cōuentus sepultus.Anno dn̄i M.cccc.xvi.kl.decembris. i Ohannes grossi patria tholosanus prior ordinis generalis.doctor diuinarū scripturarū infignis et secularis ꝑfectu nonnulla opuscula: de quibus subiecta ferūtur.Opufculū de ordinis sui institutione et ꝓfectu qd̓ p̄notauit viridariū li.iij.Sermones quoqꝫ et varie in scripturis questiones.Morit sub martino papa quīto.Anno dn̄i.M.cccc.quarto et vicesimo. Indictione secunda. t Homas walden.natione anglicus prior prouīcialis anglie.vir in diuinis scripturis studiofus et valde eruditus.et in seculari ph̓ia egregie doctus.expugnator.scripfit insigne opus cōtra wickleffitas quod p̄notauit doctrinale ecclesie.li.i.Jn multos quoqꝫ libros aristotelis comentarios fecit: qui a multis in precio habentur.Alia insuper nōn venerūt.Morit nōsine opinione sanctita tis rothomagi sepultus.Anno domini M.cccc.xxx.

as in secular sciences, studious and learned. Ready in intellect and an acute disputant, he wrote a distinguished volume on the Sentences, eight books; Sermons for the season, one book; also Sermons on the saints, one book; Questions of philosophy. But he also composed certain other works, which have not come to me.

Stephen the Englishman, doctor of Oxford and provincial prior of England, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, adorned no less by life than by learning, wrote Against the Lollards, one book; notable Sermons, both for the season and on the saints, through the cycle of the year, two books; also various Questions, one book; a Repertory of his arguments, one book. He also published certain notable lectures on books of the Bible, along with many other things that are unknown to me.

Arnold of Austria, German by nation, of the convent of Vienna, and doctor of the university of the same city, very learned in the divine Scriptures and notably taught in secular philosophy; subtle in intellect and an outstanding disputant of scholastic questions. He is said to have written some excellent little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these there is extant a distinguished volume on the Sentences, four books; also sermons and various questions. He flourished in the aforesaid university of Vienna, where he also publicly read his said lecture on the book of the Sentences.

Johannes Brammart, German by nation, of the convent of Aachen, provincial prior of Lower Germany, doctor of Paris, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures; subtle in intellect and composed in eloquence, devout in life and conduct, wrote a distinguished work on the Sentences, containing four books, which he completed at Paris in the year of the Lord 1380, in the third indiction. It begins thus: “The word of the Lord upon John.” Also sermons and various questions. He died in the convent of Cologne and was buried there, in the year of the Lord 1407, in the fifteenth indiction.

Michael of Bologna, Italian by nation, prior general, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, distinguished in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote many excellent little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Sentences, three books; also Questions on the Sentences, one book; Table of the Sentences, one book; on the whole Psalter, a large work, one book; On the Gospel of Matthew, one book; On the Gospel of Luke, one book; Table of the Moralia of Pope Gregory on Job, one book; Table on the Decretum, one book; On the Most Pure Conception of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin, one book; Various Sermons, one book; a notable Lenten collection, one book. He also wrote commentaries on many books of Aristotle; also on Valerius Maximus. In philosophy, in canon law, and in oratory likewise he wrote various works. And many other things that have not come to me. He died at Bologna, buried before the high altar of his convent, in the year of the Lord 1416, on the Kalends of December.

Johannes Grossi, by homeland a Toulousain, prior general of the order, a distinguished doctor of the divine Scriptures and fully trained in secular [letters?], wrote some little works, of which the following are reported: a little work on the institution and progress of his order, which he entitled Viridarium, three books; also sermons and various questions on the Scriptures. He died under Pope Martin V, in the year of the Lord 1424, in the second indiction.

Thomas Walden, English by nation, provincial prior of England, a man studious and very learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently taught in secular philosophy, an assailant, wrote a distinguished work against the Wycliffites, which he entitled the Doctrinale of the Church, one book. He also made commentaries on many books of Aristotle, which are held in esteem by many. Other works besides have not come to me. He died, not without a reputation for holiness, buried at Rouen, in the year of the Lord 1430.

25

Ohannes soreth natione normannus.prior totius ordinis generalis: vir in diuinis scripturis doctus et eruditus. ingenio subtilis.sermone cōpositus.vita et conuersatione deuotus atqꝫ sanctissimus:maximus et feruentissimꝰ sui ordinis reformator ꝓ cuius institucōne et multos et duros labores patientissime sustinuit:scripsit quedā p̄clara volumina: quibꝫ venā ingeniij suis etiā posteris notificauit.Equibꝫ subiecta serūtur.Super sententias li.uij.Sermones varij li.i.In regulā ordinis sui duplex cōmentū edidit li.ij.Cōstitucōnes quoqꝫ eiusdē ordinis cōportauit.Moritur andegauis sub friderico imperatore tercio.et sexto papa quarto.Anno domini .M.cccc.lxxi.Jndictione quarta.octauo kl̓.augusti.multis quotidie miraculis choruscans. In the eighth indiction, on the third day before the Nones of November.

John Bernega, English by nation, a doctor most learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally well taught in secular letters, of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people and in disputing questions of the Scriptures, wrote a distinguished work on the Sentences, in three books, and certain other things. He flourished under Pope Eugenius IV, in the year of the Lord 1430.

Michael Herbrant of Düren, German by nation, prior of the convent of Kreuznach, a man zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures and renowned for experience in many matters, outstanding in talent and an excellent preacher of the word of God, wrote certain little works not to be despised in reading, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there survive many notable sermons, one book; also many and varied conferences delivered in chapters and synods, one book. The rest that he composed have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Rupert the Bavarian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1410.

John Gauwer, German by nation, lector of the convent of Mainz, zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, wrote certain distinguished little works, of which I have found the following: On the Sentences, four books; On Exodus, one book; One Gospel from the Four, one book; Sermons on the season, one book; also Sermons on the saints, one book; a Lenten book, one book. The other things he composed have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Sigismund in the year of the Lord 1430, and was buried in his convent at Mainz.

Jacob of Reggio, Italian by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and magnificently imbued with secular letters, skilled in the three principal languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, renowned in talent and eloquent in speech, excelling in verse and prose, wrote notable sermons for Lent, one book. He is also said to have written many things in verse, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1460.

John Soreth, Norman by nation, prior general of the whole order, a man learned and trained in the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent, composed in speech, devout and most holy in life and conduct, the greatest and most fervent reformer of his order, for whose establishment he very patiently endured many hard labors, wrote certain distinguished volumes by which he made the vein of his talent known also to his posterity. Of these the following are preserved: On the Sentences, seven books; Various Sermons, one book. On the rule of his order he published a twofold commentary, two books. He also compiled the constitutions of the same order. He died at Angers under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1471, in the fourth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, shining daily with many miracles.

Oswin Hex, from Brabant by homeland, of the convent of Vlissingen, bishop of Hierapolis, vicar in pontificals of the bishop of Utrecht, a man exceptionally learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent and renowned in eloquence, very learned in delivering sermons to the people, wrote On the Ten Commandments, one book; Directory of a Troubled Conscience, one book; Sermons on the season, one book; Sermons on the saints, one book; and certain other things. He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1475, in the seventh indiction, on the Kalends of April.

John Beets, German by nation, of the convent of Tienen, a very celebrated doctor of sacred letters and much learned in secular philosophy, subtle in talent and renowned in eloquence, an acute disputant, and an excellent preacher of the word, venerable no less for his conduct than for his learning, wrote for the edification of the brethren certain distinguished volumes, among which the following are preserved: On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, one book; Preceptorium of the Divine Law, ten books; On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book; Sermons on the season, one book; also Sermons on the saints, one book; Various Disputed Questions, one book; and certain other things. He died in the year of the Lord 1486.

26
.xvi.kl.augusti. Alterus hont natione anglicus. vir in diuinis scripturis valde eruditus.et secularium lr̄aꝝ non ignarus: ingenio subtilis.scientia profundus:stu dio et exercitacōne lectionis continuus: fertur nonnulla p̄clara scripsisse opuscula : quibus memoriā sui posteris cōmeudauit.E quibus extat opus insigne super senten¬ tias li.iij.De pauꝑtate christi li.i.Alia infup qͣ multa cō posuisse dicitur: que ad noticiā meā nō venerūt.Claruit sub fixto papa quarto Anno dn̄i.M.cccc.lxxx.Etnescio si adbuc viuat. Aulus biscontus nicolai papequinti quondam confessor: vir in diuinis scripturis iugi studio ex ercitatus et eruditus ingenio subtilis. et clarus eloquio:fertur de varijs rebus multa scripisse opusculaq̃ quibus nomen fuū posteris notificauit.Ego tamen vsqʒ in hūc diem nihil eorum potui inuenire.Claruit Annodomi- nī.Millefimo.cccc.xl. Ohannes de dufeldorp.natione theutonicus. conuentus maguntineuf .et prior argentinef . vir in diuinis scripturus studiosus et doctor val¬ de eruditus : ingenio promptus et clarus eloquio.in de¬ clandis ad populū sermonibus facundus et multum idoneus.vita et cōuersatione deuotus: et regularis disci pline cuftos etamator precipuus.Scripfit de obseruan tia dierū festorū li.i.Itinerariū terre fancte quā p̄fonali¬ ter visitauit li.i.Sermones varios de tempore et de fan¬ ctis li.ij.Et alia complura.Moritur in cōuentu suo ar¬ gentinenfi sepultus.Anno domini.Milefino.cxiiij. Indictionevero.xij. Ohannes consobrinus.patria portugalenfis. vir in diuinis scrtpturis eruditissimus : et secula rium litterarū non ignarus.theologus.phius ac iurista celeberrimꝰ:ingenio subtilis et clarus elq̃ quio: declamator sermonū egregius: qui multa contra E ij hereticos fortiter gessit ꝓ christi amore. scripsit ad instan tiā prepositi regalis collegij diue marie de amhten in anglia opus triꝑtitū insigne de cōtractibʒ et cōmutationibʒ quod p̄notauit de iusticia cōmutatiua.li.uij.Sermones quoqꝫ varios.Et quedā alia.Conflatū francisci marnis grato compendio abbreuiauit.Claruit Anno dn̄i.M.cccc.lxxv.Et sub fixto pontifice quarto.vlixbone nō fine veneni potati opinione mortē subiijt. Ohannes de arundine.natione theutonicus.cō uentus brugenẜ.ep̄s vsbitenẜ.vir in diuinis scripturis eruditus.et in seculari ph̕ia egregie doctus.declamator sermonū celeberrimus.ingenio subtilis.eloquio et cōuersatione clarus:scripsit multa p̄clara opuscula quibus nomen suu͂ longe notificauit.De quibʒ ferūtur subiecta.Lectura notabilis in librū sapientie.li.i.In epistolā pauli ad romanos li.i.Sermones de tꝑe.li.i.Sermones de sanctoris.li.i.Alia quoqꝫ multa scripsisse dicit᷑:que ad noticiā meā non venerūt.Viuit adhuc in vrbe traiectensii vicaarius ep̄i in pontificalibus ibidem existens. Aptista ferrarienẜ.vir in divinis scripturis eru ditus:et in secularibus lr̄is egregie doctus.metro excellens et prosa.vtriusqꝫ lingue peritus:in declamādis sermonibʒ ad populū excellētis ingenij:scripsit ml̕ta instructa volumīa.quibʒ nomen suū longe lateqꝫ diuuulgauit.Opus luculentissimū historiarū a christi natuitate vsqꝫ ad nostra tꝑa qd̓ floridā p̄notauit.Cronica quoqꝫ sui ordinis li.i.De ruina romani imperij.li.i.Uita mechtilidis.li.ij.Cronica ferrarienisiū.li.i.Sermones varij.li.iij.Multae pigrāmata duierso genere metri cōposuit.Con uertit de greco in latinū cōplures sermones beati iohannis crysostoni.Et alia plura nobis incognita.Viuit vsqꝫ hodie apud ferrariam:et varia conscribit.

on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August.

[Walterus Hont?], English by nation, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, profound in knowledge, continuous in his study and practice of reading, is said to have written some excellent little works, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Of these there survives a distinguished work on the Sentences, three books; On the Poverty of Christ, one book. He is said to have composed many other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480. And I do not know whether he is still alive.

Aulus Biscontus, once confessor of Pope Nicholas V, a man exercised and learned in the divine Scriptures by constant study, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, is said to have written many little works on various subjects, by which he made his name known to posterity. I, however, up to this day have been able to find none of them. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1440.

Johannes de Dufeldorp, German by nation, of the convent of Mainz and prior of Strasbourg, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and a very learned doctor, ready in intellect and clear in speech, eloquent and very capable in delivering sermons to the people, devout in life and conduct, and an outstanding guardian and lover of regular discipline, wrote On the Observance of Feast Days, one book; An Itinerary of the Holy Land, which he visited in person, one book; various sermons on the season and on the saints, two books; and many other things. He died in his own convent of Strasbourg and was buried there, in the year of the Lord 1114, in the twelfth indiction.

Johannes Consobrinus, by homeland Portuguese, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, a very celebrated theologian, philosopher, and jurist, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, who did many things bravely against heretics for love of Christ, wrote, at the request of the provost of the royal college of St Mary of [Amhten?] in England, a distinguished tripartite work on contracts and exchanges, which he entitled On Commutative Justice, seven books; various sermons also; and certain other things. He abridged the Conflatus of Franciscus Maronis in a pleasing compendium. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1475, and under Pope Sixtus IV; at Lisbon he underwent death, not without suspicion that poison had been drunk.

Johannes de Arundine, German by nation, of the convent of Bruges, bishop of Us [unclear], a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently taught in secular philosophy, a very celebrated declaimer of sermons, subtle in intellect, clear in speech and conduct, wrote many excellent little works, by which he made his name widely known. Of these the following are reported: a notable lecture on the Book of Wisdom, one book; on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, one book; sermons on the season, one book; sermons on the saints, one book. He is said to have written many other things also, which have not come to my knowledge. He is still living in the city of Utrecht, being the bishop’s vicar there in pontifical matters.

Baptista of Ferrara, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently taught in secular letters, outstanding in verse and prose, skilled in both languages, of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, wrote many well-instructed volumes, by which he made his name known far and wide: a most lucid work of histories from the nativity of Christ down to our own times, which he entitled Florida; a chronicle also of his order, one book; On the Fall of the Roman Empire, one book; The Life of Mechtilde, two books; a chronicle of the Ferrarese, one book; various sermons, three books. He composed many epigrams in different kinds of meter. He translated from Greek into Latin several sermons of blessed John Chrysostom, and many other things unknown to us. He is living to this day at Ferrara, and is writing various works.

Johannes Wiric of Nussia, a German by nation, of the convent of Cologne, provincial prior of Lower Germany, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, ready in intellect and clear in speech, a famous preacher of the divine word, is reported by those who knew him to have written on the Sentences, eight books; various sermons and conferences, which in their time will come forth into the light. He is still living in his convent at Cologne, composing various works.

Johannes Placentinus, a man most learned in every respect, a theologian and very celebrated rhetorician, ready in intellect and eloquent in speech, most skilled in the Greek and Latin languages, since he translated many things elegantly, is reported to have written several little works by which he consecrated his name to immortality. Of these I have seen only: a Greek Vocabulary, a work truly useful and necessary, one book. There is also another smaller volume of his, where Latin is set before Greek, one book. To Ludovicus Donatus, bishop of Bergamo, he translated the Psalter from Greek word for word with the greatest exactness; no one can praise this work worthily enough. In it he first set down the Greek translation in Greek letters, and appended his own in Latin letters. He composed many elegant letters to various persons. He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Pope Innocent VIII, and I believe that he is still living.

Johannes Scandeberius, bishop of Erford in England, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, devout also in life and conduct, is reported to have written many distinguished little works by which he made his name known far and wide. But I do not remember that any of them has come to my knowledge. He flourished in England under Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480. I do not know whether he is still living.

Baptista Mantuanus, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and, in the knowledge of secular letters, second to none in this age; an eminent doctor of sacred theology, priest, orator, and very celebrated poet; subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, skilled in both languages, namely Greek and Latin; one who equals Virgil in verse and Cicero in prose, not to say surpasses them. He wrote many excellent volumes in both kinds of style, by which he acquired for his name celebrated fame throughout the whole Christian world. Among these the following are reported: Dialogue on the Blessed Life, to his father, one book; Suburbanus, in verse, on bucolic matters, one book; On the Praises of Saint Mary, Parthenices, three books; On Saint Katherine the Martyr, one book; On the Life of Saint Albert of his order, in Sapphic verse, one book; On the Calamity of These Times, or On the Capital Sins, in heroic verse, a most elegant work, one book; Panegyric of Robert, one book; Dream concerning the same, one book; To Falcon, a varied work of epigrams, which he entitled Falcon, one book; Consolation on Death, one book; On Contempt of Death, one book; Against Poets Writing Shameful Things, one book; To Pope Innocent VIII, On the Capture of Granada, four books; On Patience, one book; On the Origin and Diversity of Religious Orders, one book; Apology for Brother Peter, two books; Introduction to the Subtle Scotus, one book; elegant and various Orations, one book. He wrote almost innumerable letters to various persons. He also published countless and most elegant poems of various kinds, which in their time will come forth into the light. Indeed he is so ready and elegant a versifier that he has never had his equal, if you direct your mind to the majesty of his poetry and to his knowledge of all philosophy and learning. He lives to this day in Italy, the unique glory of the Carmelite order, the prince of learned men, and he is composing many works to be published day by day.

Arnoldus Bostius, a German by nation, of the convent of Ghent in Flanders, a man most zealous in the divine Scriptures and very learned, and excellently instructed in secular letters; ready in intellect and clear in speech; an eminent theologian, philosopher, and poet; practiced in verse and prose; devout in life and conduct, and a chief lover and guardian of regular discipline, wrote certain distinguished little works in verse and prose, by which his name

he became known. Of these the following are reported: a prose volume, mixed with verses inserted, which he entitled On the Patronage of the Mother of God, of the Carmelite Order, one book; On the Illustrious Men of His Order, one book; On the Illustrious Men of the Carthusians, one book; On the Most Pure Conception of the Mother of God and Virgin Mary, against Vincentius of Novo Castro, one book; On the Four Last Things, one book. He also published various sermons, and many letters both to me and to others, the number of which is uncertain. He also published several poems on various subjects. He composed some other works as well, which have not come to our knowledge. He is still living at Ghent, composing various works and stirring many to the study of letters.

Johannes de Aqua Veteri, German by nation, Brabantine by homeland, of the convent of Mechelen, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and skilled by long practice, of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, and a zealous and devout lover of his order, wrote, at the urgent request and for the edification of many brothers, a commendable work on the beginning, progress, and state of his order, which he entitled A Three-Part Bundle of the Times of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, three books. In the first of these he proves that Elijah and the prophets were the founders of his order; in the second he enumerates the saints and canonized persons from the same order; in the third he sets out, according to the times, the successions of the priors general of his whole order. But the other works which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge. He is still living in the convent of Aachen, and strongly perseveres in the study he has begun, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1492, indiction 10.

Apology of the author for the fact that not all the doctors and writers of this order who wrote have been inserted here.

From these most learned men, therefore, of whom we have made mention, reader, you can recognize how great you ought to judge the fruits of Carmel to be. But we have extracted a few from many, whose talents and writings we have known. Nor do we doubt that there remain several most learned men of this order, who, flourishing at various times, magnificently adorned it by their talents and writings, but whose memory has not reached us. For the Carmelite religion is older than all orders, and that very great antiquity has easily brought the bright lights of its own into oblivion. Therefore, whoever desires to know more fruitful shoots of Mount Carmel should read the deeds and histories of the same order, and he will be able to find most learned men of whom there has been no mention in this catalogue. For, having obtained neither the time nor the leisure to search out the others who are lacking, we have therefore arranged these in order, so that we might provide the reader with an occasion for investigating the rest. Finally, to you, brothers, cultivators of the Carmelite order, we turn our mind; to your charities we offer the present gift, and, in return for our devoted love, we earnestly beseech you to pray to God for us.

Elegiac Poem of Lord Johannes Tritemius, Abbot, Addressing His Carmelite Book.

Go now, dear book; present yourself to the venerable fathers, in whose praise you have been created and are present. Do not fear to see men learned and honorable in morals, and renowned with a devout mind. There is no reason for you to be afraid: the men are friendly and sweet and gentle; you may approach them boldly. Among such men above all, remember to carry my greeting, and do not hesitate; I promise you will be welcome. If anyone is pricked by the goads of envy, pay no heed. If anyone seeks to gnaw you with his tooth, flee. Always in adversities the patient man wins glorious trophies; the impatient man carries off shameful reproaches. The impious and depraved man speaks evils shut up in his heart; such things, my book, I beg you not to fear.

For the fathers of the gracious order will indeed defend you, whom Mary, the Virgin, mother of the Lord, cherishes. Carmel, the famous mountain, gave to these fathers an apt name by its religion. O holy mountain, now you duly behold your followers, and the sacred order endures steadfast continually. Whoever there shall be [unclear] who venerates you with honor, cherish him, grateful, with special love. If anyone looks upon you with a bitter, harsh face, indignant, flee of your own accord from his hands. The press calls you, easily to be printed, so that, sweet one, you may be able to be useful to men. Yet observe that you are not changed, nor ever fall out of agreement with my pen and my meanings. As my reward I ask your fathers for prayers poured out to the Lord, that he may purge every sin.

Of Johannes Empolidis, canon of Saint Peter of Dumentum, on the book of lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, On the Praise of the Order of Carmelites.

In the present volume are praised the lights of the sacred order, which the gracious mother holds and cherishes. Carmel the mountain gave these fathers their name; thence flows all the glory of the Carmelites. Famous antiquity of this order, and holy life, brought distinguished titles to the brothers. The Trithemian pen adorns them, brothers, with worthy praises, and does not allow them to be in gloomy places. For the increase of the praise of so bright a religion, with wondrous talent he gathers all things ancient, and urges the new to advance along the path of the old. Nor does he spare the venerable ancient customs of the fathers, but strikes such men sharply with the sword of the word. Thus he approves the noble by their merits or gracious deeds, so that by his writings he may call the frail to better things.

Thus is the custom of experienced teachers of the young: that the rest of the company may learn by the praise of one. With this ready spirit, reader, receive my poem, and read the approved beginnings of the famous volume.

Poem of Rutgerus Venrai, a Sicambrian regular in Heyna, on the book of lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot, On the Praise of the Order of Carmelites.

The poets of old were accustomed to praise the gods in verses, and with the lyre resounding and sounding again. But what thing not blameworthy, not vain, not wicked, did they, anxious in their talents, not compose? Turn over the books, reader, and the great volumes of the ancient bards: you will find many frivolous things sung. Look at Virgil: you will often see there warlike, spirited goddesses, Juno and Venus. The famous book of Homer relates many invented things; nothing is sincere, nothing weighty, and nothing pious. The excellent Plautus, and also sharp Terence, approve decorous things with unchaste games. Let Pamphilus fall silent; let Maximianus yield; and let Naso cease to play with unequal meters. These [unclear] the fire [unclear] halls with modulated songs, and do not allow young men to be of chaste morals. Our Trithemius, not following vain trifles, strives to raise men with excellent praise: not just any men, but men distinguished by gracious morals, by various arts, and by weighty uprightness, and deservedly called fellow-brothers of the gracious Virgin, who stood out in their life and merits. For their ancient religion the fathers deserved surpassing praise before all [unclear]. Now bright knowledge has joined itself with ancient morals, and wages war with uprightness. Not that it overcomes it; rather it is overcome by it: what was ancient remains unviolated.

For one may see not a few of this order no less skilled in art than upright in goodness. Seeing these things, lord Trithemius, the renowned abbot, has, behold, published two distinguished books. He touched upon the excellent fathers, the praises of the gracious order, and the old and new customs. Carmelite, now give thanks to your poet; for he has made you shine forth from the shadows.

A Sapphic Poem by the Same on the Same Subject.

Behold, those to whom Carmel is shown to have given the name, and the mother of the Lord, in this book receive the praises of an ancient religious order.

A distinguished man, the abbot of Sponheim, Johannes, published it with a fair pen, skilled in Latin, Hebrew, and Greek letters.

The brothers and masters of the duly consecrated order, bright in morals, fair in uprightness, shining with the light of doctrine, he approves as a glittering choir.

Therefore the venerable abbot commends the brothers of Mary with great praises, so that, mindful of their ancient honor, they may avoid shameful things.

He has resolved that the frail should always be rebuked more sparingly, the modest more strongly and justly approved, as this little book bears witness.

I judge that the fathers of this sacred order will readily be grateful to him, now shining out from black decay and blind shadows.

Printed at Mainz.
